subject: Japan
note: Cited to a pinned Wikipedia revision (trusted_secondary): Seikan Tunnel. Lengths and depths are quoted as the page states them. The portal points are the page's infobox coordinates (Shiriuchi, Hokkaido; Imabetsu, Aomori on Honshu). If an elevation profile is drawn it is computed from NOAA ETOPO 2022 along the line between the portals and shows the strait floor, not the tunnel; the tunnel depth must come only from the page's figures (about 100 m below the seabed and 240 m below sea level). Hokkaido, Honshu and the Tsugaru Strait are not named places in the map data; the portals are the points to frame.

claims.text: The Seikan Tunnel is a 53.85 km dual-gauge railway tunnel in Japan, with a 23.3 km segment running beneath the seabed of the Tsugaru Strait, which separates Aomori Prefecture on Honshu from Hokkaido.
The tunnel's track level lies approximately 100 m below the seabed and 240 m below sea level.
The tunnel opened on 13 March 1988, after several decades of planning and construction.
By total length the Seikan Tunnel is the world's longest undersea tunnel, surpassing the Channel Tunnel, though the Channel Tunnel has the longer undersea section, 37.9 km against 23.3 km.
It is the deepest railway tunnel below sea level, and was the deepest transport tunnel of any kind until Norway's Hitra Tunnel opened in 1994.
In 1954 five ferries, including the Toya Maru, sank in the Tsugaru Strait during a typhoon, killing 1,430 passengers.
Drilling began in 1972 from both sides, and 34 workers were killed during construction. To avoid danger from earthquakes the tunnel goes through dense volcanic rock.
Ferry traffic predictions made in 1971 were overestimates: traffic peaked in 1978, earlier than predicted, and then decreased, and the ferry was mostly supplanted by air travel.
The tunnel forms part of the standard-gauge Hokkaido Shinkansen as well as the narrow-gauge Kaikyo Line, and has two tracks.
